a.xlink:title: Take the uniform supremum over convex sets after bounding their perimeter.

Apply the theorem to the snowflake boundary tube estimate.
Divide each discrepancy bound by the area at the stated shrinking scales.
Apply the convex variance clause and Chebyshev's inequality after dividing by the square of the test-set area.
Apply the disc variance clause at a geometric grid of radii, then use a union bound and monotonicity.
Apply Chebyshev's inequality with the disc variance clause (1.14) to centers of empty discs.
Sum the input over the dyadic ranges 2^j≤|r|<2^(j+1), including the final block when R is a power of two.
Use R=MN/d²≥1 and Y=X/d≥1; the remaining d-weights are d^−2 and d^−1.

Use the integral-error and shell-energy bounds of the brackets.
Pointwise upper and lower brackets are valid at every difference point, including boundary points.
The proof's bound P<=4 controls the small-power factor in the large-perimeter regime.
Use the perimeter bound P<=4 established in Lemma 2.7's proof.
Insert specifically (2.17), (2.19), and (2.20) into the bracket bounds, with s=3δ≤1.
Use the convex Fourier tail (2.19), pointwise coefficient bound (2.20), and bounded perimeter.

Integral error and the pointwise bracket coefficient bound in (2.21).
Reuse only the boundary-crossing argument; the alpha-power translation estimate is derived here, without invoking the remark's linear conclusion.
Use Proposition 3.1(i), the smooth counting identity (3.1), for each bracket.
The difference-measure identity (3.2) expresses the smooth count through nonnegative squared coefficients.
Use the difference-measure Fourier identity (3.2) in the product-bracket reduction.
Use the indicator variance identity (3.3) without smoothing.
Use the indicator variance identity (3.3).
Sum the four shell contributions, whose exponents stay away from zero in this convex calculation.
Use the compact-range uniform bound explicitly established in the lemma's proof for the three safe exponents; derive the remaining near-zero case separately.
Sum the decaying dyadic frequency terms before choosing the smoothing scale.
Control S_1 and its smoothing dependence in the one-variable block sums.
Choose delta according to the large- and small-perimeter regimes and absorb the small powers.
Gives the upper bound uniformly for perimeter at most p.
Use the pairwise coordinate separation and the perimeter-to-width argument from the proof of Proposition 4.3.
Supplies the width-sensitive elementary bound.
Products of arc brackets have factorized coefficients and a controlled integral error.
Establishes the exact identity (1.15) and its stated sufficient conditions.
Handle the regime P below 2 X to the minus two by the exact one-point variance.
Handle a side shorter than X to the minus two by the exact identity.
BRS Theorem 1.3 supplies the fixed-height dyadic frequency moment; Section 2.1 supplies the small-power convention.
The cited elementary proof supplies Selberg's identity; the manuscript also records Selberg's attribution and Kuznetsov as a proof reference.
Equation (1.81) supplies τ(v)≪ηv^η.
Equation (3.2) gives the Ramanujan-sum divisor formula; the manuscript also indicates its elementary Möbius-inversion derivation.
Theorem 330 supplies the summatory totient asymptotic used to normalize the point-set coefficients.
Parseval converts the L² translation norm into a nonnegative Fourier multiplier sum.
Converts the full Fourier energy of the difference indicator into its L² norm.
Apply Parseval to the bounded measurable finite reflected-translate sum Z_E.
Absolutely convergent pointwise smooth Fourier inversion justifies summation over the finite point set.
Apply the same smooth Fourier inversion to the finite difference average.
Fourier coefficients of the convolution are products of the mollifier and set coefficients.
Divide the finite exponential sum by its number of unit-modulus summands.
Identifies each finite exponential sum with N_Xa_X(k).
Factor the double exponential sum into a_X(k) times its complex conjugate.
Identifies its nonzero Fourier coefficients as a_X(−k) times the reflected indicator coefficient.
Divide by N_X²≫X⁴ in the shell second moment.
The lower bound N_X>>X^2 normalizes the coordinate count.
The comparison N_X much greater than X squared converts the unnormalized frequency moment to normalized coefficients.
Turn the exact error at most N_X inverse into O(X to the minus two).
Bound A/N_X by a constant times A X to the minus two in the one-point case.
Normalize the rectangular frequency moment and bound V/N_X in the one-point case.
Supplies the stated pointwise bound 0≤|a_X(k)|²≤1.
The zero coefficient is a_X(0)=1; |a_X(k)|≤1 also preserves absolute convergence.
The zero-frequency term is the integral and the weighted series is absolutely convergent.
Controls the variance series by the indicator's L² Fourier energy.
The estimate |a_X(k)| at most one lets the geometric Fourier tail control all frequencies above T.
Interchange the frequency arguments to obtain the same bound on the second axis.
Sum over c≤X and write c=dℓ, restricting d≤X.
Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to the divisor sum before summing over off-axis frequencies.
Bound the number of divisors and the at most 2τ(|r|) signed factorizations uv=r.
After |A_X(0,n)|≤Xτ(|n|), sum the squared divisor estimate on both axes.
Supplies the off-axis bound; its logarithm is absorbed by choosing η=ε/4.
Add both axis contributions to the off-axis estimate.
Identifies the multiplier |e(k·h)−1|² before averaging over the square Q_H.
The selected shift makes the Fourier multiplier exactly −2.
Defines the positive normalized smooth mollifier, gives pointwise enclosure, and supplies the Fourier cutoff factor.
Use the same periodization and integration-by-parts argument for a one-dimensional smooth mollifier.
Bounds a translation symmetric difference by an arbitrarily slightly larger boundary neighborhood; subdivision removes the quadratic term.
Both smoothing-set differences are supported in the 3δ boundary neighborhood.
Controls the integral error and both the L¹ Fourier-coefficient error and L² Fourier-energy error.
Cover the rectifiable boundary by short arcs and project the Euclidean tube to the torus.
Uses the convex boundary's perimeter and nullness to justify slicing and periodization of the closure.
Supplies the boundary-neighborhood estimate (2.17), including degenerate cases.
Supplies the symmetric-difference estimate (2.18), including degenerate cases.
Supplies the translation hypothesis with α=1 and Λ=P.
The special shift h=k/(2|k|₂²) bounds the L¹ difference by P/(2|k|₂).
Supplies the Fourier tail (2.19) and its shell consequence.
Supplies the area/perimeter coefficient bound (2.20).
Supplies the corresponding separately proved component of the proposition.
Supplies the corresponding separately proved component of the proposition.
Supplies the corresponding separately proved component of the proposition.
Fourier coefficients of the indicator depend only on its L² class.
Identifies the desired squared L² norm with the symmetric-difference measure.
The squared L² translation bound also controls the L¹ norm needed for a single coefficient.
Reduce convex discrepancy to bracket Fourier sums and the integral errors.
Apply the same valid generic bracket reduction with the new boundary integral error.
Count lifted points using each coordinate width.
The thin rectangle contains order-X reciprocal points, so their normalized mass is of order at least X^-1.
Normalize the explicit segment count with N_X<=X^2.
The packing argument uses the elementary upper bound N_X <= X^2, repeated at this location.
Supplies the matching lower bound, including p=0 and real X.
Supplies the set-dependent shell norm and the boundary approximation error.
Sum uniformly through the possible zero exponent and retain the necessary logarithmic factor.
Optimize delta and bound the remaining terms uniformly in alpha and B; treat B>=X^alpha trivially.
Verifies the boundary theorem's hypothesis with alpha=1 and B=8(1+gamma).
Any gamma-well-shaped set would satisfy the linear tube bound already proved for Corollary 4.6; the dimension contradicts it.
The tube upper estimate supplies alpha=2-d, while the dimension information rules out linear tube growth.
Use BRS's Euclidean definition of gamma-well-shapedness; the torus tube estimate itself is proved here.
Use the Koch construction arcs and Minkowski dimension from LP Section 1.
Establishes the convex clause (1.9).
Combine the explicit arc coefficient with the mollifier multiplier.
Use the explicit unsmoothed arc indicator coefficients and their product factorization.
Establishes the product-of-arcs clause (1.10).
Reuse the dyadic blocks and factorized summation from the rectangle difference proof; no use is made of its final discrepancy bound.
Control the change of normalization and removal of the equal-point pairs.
Establishes the convex variance clause (1.12).
Specialize the already established convex bound to area pi r squared and perimeter 2 pi r.
Establishes the disc variance clause (1.14).
Establishes the rectangle variance clause (1.13).
Use the empty rectangle's central subrectangle to obtain measure of order X inverse at distance of order X to the minus one half.
Bound the intermediate-radius tail in the layer-cake integral.
Truncate the distance-tail integral uniformly at X to the minus one half plus kappa.
Establishes the upper half of (1.16) for all s greater than zero.
Combines the packing and empty-rectangle lower bounds to select the exponent min(s,1+s/2).
Credit the empty-box construction; lines 225–229 verify the particular rectangle directly.
For convex sets represented inside a translated unit square, bounds discrepancy by $X^{\varepsilon}(X^{-1}+P^{2/3}X^{-2/3})$, uniformly in the position and the set, for $X\ge2$.
Taking the supremum over the manuscript's class of convex sets gives discrepancy $\ll_{\varepsilon}X^{-2/3+\varepsilon}$.

For a fixed convex body of positive area and $0<\kappa<1/2$, obtains relative error $O_{K_0,\kappa}(X^{-\kappa})$ at dilations $t\ge X^{-1/2+\kappa}$ that fit inside a translated unit square, uniformly over translations and rotations.
If $b_E(s)\le Bs^{\alpha}$ for $0<s\le1$, $0<\alpha\le1$ and $B\ge1$, gives $D_X(E)\ll_{\varepsilon}B^{2/(2+\alpha)}X^{-2\alpha/(2+\alpha)+\varepsilon}$ for $X\ge2$.

The difference measure, including diagonal pairs, has discrepancy $\ll_\varepsilon X^\varepsilon(PX^{-1}+X^{-2})$ for a convex set of perimeter $P$ in a translated unit square. For a product of arcs of area $V$, the bound is $\ll_\varepsilon X^\varepsilon(X^{-2}+V^{2/3}X^{-5/3})$, independently of its aspect ratio.

The variance of the normalized count is $\ll_\varepsilon X^\varepsilon(P^2X^{-2}+A^{4/3}P^{2/3}X^{-5/3})$ for a convex set with area $A$ and perimeter $P$. Products of arcs satisfy $\ll_\varepsilon X^\varepsilon(VX^{-2}+V^{5/3}X^{-5/3})$, and discs satisfy $\ll_\varepsilon X^\varepsilon(r^2X^{-2}+r^{10/3}X^{-5/3})$. If every translate contains at most one point, the variance equals $|E|/N_X-|E|^2$.

For every fixed $s>0$, the $s$-th distance moment lies between constant multiples of $X^{-\vartheta(s)}$ and $X^{-\vartheta(s)+\varepsilon}$, where $\vartheta(s)=\min\{s,1+s/2\}$. Thus the exponents change at $s=2$.
For all real $N,X\ge1$ and $\eta>0$, $\sum_{N\le|r|<2N}|A_X(r,1)|^2\ll_\eta(NX)^\eta(NX^2+N^{1/3}X^{7/3})$. Both signs are included, with no relation between $N$ and $X$.
For real $R,Y\ge1$, the sum over $1\le|r|\le R$ is $\ll_\eta(RY)^\eta(RY^2+R^{1/3}Y^{7/3})$.
For $M,N,X\ge1$, $\sum_{|m|\le M,\ |n|\le N,\ (m,n)\ne(0,0)}|A_X(m,n)|^2\ll_\varepsilon(MNX)^\varepsilon\{MNX^2+(MN)^{1/3}X^{7/3}\}$. The axes and all signs are included.
For $X\ge2$ and $H\ge1$, the shell $\ell^2$ norm is $\ll_\eta(HX)^\eta(X^{-1}H+X^{-5/6}H^{1/3})$. Its square is $\ll_\eta(HX)^\eta(X^{-2}H^2+X^{-5/3}H^{2/3})$, and $|a_X(k)|^2\le1$.

Translation to Fourier tails
[Pending]ambda H^{-\alpha}/[2(1-1/\pi)]$ for every real $H\ge1$.

For measurable $E\subset\mathbb T^2$ and $0<\delta\le1/8$, constructs smooth real $f_-\le\mathbf1_E\le f_+$ at every point, with values in $[0,1]$. The integral error is at most $b_E(3\delta)$; Fourier coefficients and shell norms gain $(1+\delta H)^{-L}$ with boundary errors $b_E(3\delta)$ and $b_E(3\delta)^{1/2}$ respectively.

For convex $\Omega\subset u+[0,1)^2$, $E=\pi\Omega$, perimeter $P$ and area $A$, proves $b_E(s)\le4\pi(Ps+s^2)$, $\|\mathbf1_E(\cdot+h)-\mathbf1_E\|_2^2\le P|h|_2$, Fourier tail $\ll P/T$, and $|\widehat{\mathbf1_E}(k)|\le\min(A,P/(4|k|_2))$ for $k\ne0$. Degenerate convex sets are included.

For $0<\delta\le1/8$ and $H\ge1$, with $b=P\delta+\delta^2$, the brackets have integral error $\ll b$, shell norm $\ll_L(1+\delta H)^{-L}(P^{1/2}H^{-1/2}+b^{1/2})$, and coefficient bound $\ll_L(1+\delta H)^{-L}(P/H+b)$.

For any measurable $E$ with $b_E(s)\le C_0(Ps+s^2)$ for $0<s\le1$, subdivision of a translation gives $\|\mathbf1_E(\cdot+h)-\mathbf1_E\|_1\le C_0P|h|_2$ for $|h|_2<1$. The separate convex slicing argument supplies the sharper constant used in (2.20).

For $X\ge2$, smooth counting error is $\sum_{k
e0}\widehat f(k)a_X(k)$, smooth difference-distribution error is $\sum_{k
e0}\widehat f(k)|a_X(k)|^2$, and for every measurable $E$ the translation variance is $\sum_{k
e0}|\widehat{\mathbf1_E}(k)|^2|a_X(k)|^2$.

For $C_E(v)=\int\mathbf1_E(x)\mathbf1_E(x+v)\,dx$, direct expansion gives $\mathcal V_X(E)=\int C_E\,d\nu_X-|E|^2$. The variance theorem uses the Fourier variance identity directly, independently of the difference-distribution theorem.
Controls the dyadic sum of $H^s(1+\delta H)^{-L}$ by $\delta^{-s}$ for $s>0$ and by a constant for $s<0$, with $L>\max(s,0)$ and $0<\delta\le1$.
At any $0<\delta\le1/8$, controls convex discrepancy by the boundary error $b=P\delta+\delta^2$ and the Fourier contributions with scales $X^{-1}\delta^{-1/2}$ and $X^{-5/6}$.
For convex sets in a translated unit square, gives the absolute-constant bound $D_X(\pi\Omega)\ll X^{-2}+\min(w_1,w_2)\ll X^{-2}+P(\Omega)$ for $X\ge2$.
For real $X\ge4$ and $0\le p\le X^{-1}$, the largest discrepancy among convex sets of perimeter at most p has order $p+X^{-2}$, with absolute constants.

A thin rectangle containing many diagonal reciprocal points has discrepancy $\gg X^{-1}$ while its perimeter contribution is $O(X^{-4/3})$, so the baseline term in Theorem 1.1 remains necessary even for positive-area convex bodies.
For the Euclidean definition of gamma-well-shapedness inside $[0,1)^2$, gives discrepancy $\ll_{\varepsilon}(1+\gamma)^{2/3}X^{-2/3+\varepsilon}$, uniformly for $\gamma\ge0$ and $X\ge2$.
Applies the boundary theorem to a Koch snowflake inside the unit square, with $\alpha=2-\log 4/\log 3$, giving exponent $0.539\ldots$; the same domain is not gamma-well-shaped for any finite gamma.

The finite set $E=\mathcal P_X$ has indicator zero almost everywhere but discrepancy one. Thus almost-everywhere or distributional-perimeter information cannot replace the stated pointwise/topological boundary control.

An arc of length $a$ admits smooth upper and lower brackets with integral error at most $4\delta$. With $a'=\min(1,a+4\delta)$, their coefficients are $\ll_L\min\{a',(1+|m|)^{-1}\}(1+\delta|m|)^{-L}$.

For $0<\kappa<1$, a fixed positive-area convex shape at linear scale $t\ge X^{-1+\kappa}$ has relative difference-count error $O(X^{-\kappa/2})$, uniformly in position and orientation within a translated unit square. Products of arcs have the same error when their area is at least $X^{-2+\kappa}$. Both conclusions hold with and without diagonal pairs under the corresponding normalizations.

If every translate of a measurable set contains at most one point, its normalized-count variance is $|E|/N_X-|E|^2$. A sufficient condition is containment, after projection, in a strip of width below $X^{-2}$; the stated small-perimeter, narrow-rectangle and small-disc cases follow.

For a fixed positive-area convex shape at scale $t\ge X^{-1+\kappa}$, the centers with relative count error greater than $\lambda$ have measure $\ll_{K_0,\kappa}\lambda^{-2}X^{-3\kappa/2}$, uniformly over admissible rotations and scales, for $0<\kappa<1$ and $0<\lambda\le1$.

For $r_0\le r\le1/4$, a single exceptional set has measure $\ll_\varepsilon\lambda^{-3}X^\varepsilon(X^{-2}r_0^{-2}+X^{-5/3}r_0^{-2/3})$ and outside it every disc count has relative error $O(\lambda)$. Open and closed discs are included. Taking $r_0=X^{-1+\kappa}$ and $\lambda=X^{-\kappa/3}$ yields exceptional measure $\ll_\kappa X^{-\kappa/2}$ for sufficiently large $X$.
The fixed-height signed-frequency second moment used as Theorem 2.1.
Elementary proof cited for equation (2.4); v39 gives no numbered locator for this citation.
For each positive eta, tau(v)<<_eta v^eta.
The divisor expression for Ramanujan sums used to bound the coordinate axes.
Mertens's estimate gives N_X=(3/pi^2)X^2+O(X log X).
The L2 norm is the sum of squared Fourier coefficients.
Rapid coefficient decay and absolute uniform Fourier inversion for smooth torus functions.
Convolution multiplies Fourier coefficients.
The finite exponential sum over $\mathcal P_X$ equals $A_X(m,n)=\sum_{c\le X}S(m,n;c)$, with every point counted once and the modulus-one point represented by $S(m,n;1)=1$.
The point count is $N_X=\sum_{c\le X}\varphi(c)=(3/\pi^2)X^2+O(X\log X)$; in particular $N_X\asymp X^2$ for $X\ge2$.
The normalized coefficients satisfy $a_X(k)=N_X^{-1}\sum_{z\in\mathcal P_X}e(k\cdot z)$, $a_X(0)=1$ and $|a_X(k)|\le1$.
The elementary changes of variables give $S(m,n;c)=S(n,m;c)$ and $S(-m,-n;c)=S(m,n;c)$.
For integers $m,n$ and $c\ge1$, $S(m,n;c)=\sum_{d\mid\gcd(m,n,c)}d\,S(mn/d^2,1;c/d)$.
For $mn\ne0$, summing Selberg's identity over the modulus gives $A_X(m,n)=\sum_{d\mid\gcd(|m|,|n|),\,d\le X}d\,A_{X/d}(mn/d^2,1)$.
For every $\eta>0$ and integer $v\ge1$, $\tau(v)\ll_\eta v^\eta$.

Cauchy–Schwarz over divisors and at most $2\tau(|r|)$ signed factorizations $uv=r$ reduce the off-axis second moment to $\sum_{d\le\min(M,N,X)}d^2\sum_{1\le|r|\le MN/d^2}|A_{X/d}(r,1)|^2$. The cumulative input applies with $R=MN/d^2\ge1$, $Y=X/d\ge1$; the divisor sums have weights $d^{-2}$ and $d^{-1}$.

The Ramanujan formula $S(0,n;c)=\sum_{d\mid\gcd(c,n)}d\mu(c/d)$ gives $|A_X(0,n)|\le X\tau(|n|)$; symmetry gives the corresponding bound on the other axis. The divisor estimate then bounds both axes by $O_\eta(MNX^2(MN)^{2\eta})$.
With $\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^2}f(x)e(-k\cdot x)\,dx$, one has $\widehat{f(\cdot+h)}(k)=e(k\cdot h)\widehat f(k)$.

For $0<\delta\le1/8$, the periodized mollifier $\rho_\delta$ is nonnegative, has integral one and support within distance $\delta$ of zero. Integration by parts proves $|\widehat{\rho_\delta}(k)|\ll_L(1+\delta\|k\|_\infty)^{-L}$ for every $L>0$.

A shortest lifted segment joining a point of $E$ to a point of $E^c$ meets $\partial E$. Applied to the inner and outer sets used for smoothing, this places their indicator differences from $\mathbf1_E$ within the $3\delta$ boundary neighborhood.
For the inner and outer sets $E_\pm$, $\|\mathbf1_{E_\pm}-\mathbf1_E\|_1\le b_E(3\delta)$ and $\|\mathbf1_{E_\pm}-\mathbf1_E\|_2^2\le b_E(3\delta)$.

For a convex body in a unit square, the boundary is a rectifiable Jordan curve of length $P\le4$. The arc covering argument shows that it has measure zero, while convexity gives $\operatorname{int}\overline\Omega\subset\Omega$. Thus $\mathbf1_\Omega=\mathbf1_{\overline\Omega}$ almost everywhere. Degenerate sets are handled separately.

For $E=\pi\Omega$ with convex $\Omega\subset u+[0,1)^2$, $b_E(s)\le4\pi(Ps+s^2)$ for $0<s\le1$. A cover of the Euclidean boundary is projected to the torus, using $\partial E\subset\pi(\partial\overline\Omega)$ and that projection does not increase measure.

Parallel-line slicing gives $|(K+h)\triangle K|\le P|h|_2$, since the perpendicular width is at most $P/2$. Periodization then yields $\|\mathbf1_E(\cdot+h)-\mathbf1_E\|_2^2\le P|h|_2$ on the torus for every $h\in\mathbb R^2$.

The translation estimate with $Convex Fourier tailambda=P$ and $\alpha=1$ in Lemma 2.5 yields $\sum_{\|k\|_\infty\ge T}|\widehat{\mathbf1_E}(k)|^2\ll P/T$ for $T\ge1$, and hence the same bound on a dyadic shell.
For $k\ne0$, the special translation $h=k/(2|k|_2^2)$ has multiplier $-2$ and gives $|\widehat{\mathbf1_E}(k)|\le P/(4|k|_2)$. Combining this with the trivial area bound gives $\min\{A,P/(4|k|_2)\}$.
For smooth $f$, $\int f\,d\mu_X-\int f=\sum_{k\ne0}\widehat f(k)a_X(k)$, with absolute convergence. It follows by pointwise smooth Fourier inversion and a finite average over $\mathcal P_X$.
For smooth $f$, $\int f\,d\nu_X-\int f=\sum_{k\ne0}\widehat f(k)|a_X(k)|^2$, with absolute convergence. The finite double exponential sum factors as $a_X(k)\overline{a_X(k)}$.

For every measurable $E$, the finite reflected-translate sum $Z_E(u)=\mu_X(u+E)-|E|$ has nonzero Fourier coefficients $a_X(-k)\widehat{\mathbf1_E}(-k)$. Parseval gives $\mathcal V_X(E)=\sum_{k\ne0}|\widehat{\mathbf1_E}(k)|^2|a_X(k)|^2$.

The variance identity depends only on the $L^2$ class of $\mathbf1_E$, so changing $E$ on a null set leaves $\mathcal V_X(E)$ unchanged. In particular, boundary choices do not affect convex-set variance.
For an indicator, $\|\mathbf1_E(\cdot+h)-\mathbf1_E\|_2^2=\|\mathbf1_E(\cdot+h)-\mathbf1_E\|_1=|(E-h)\triangle E|$.
Pointwise upper and lower brackets reduce discrepancy to the larger smooth counting Fourier sum plus their integral error. The same reduction applies to general measurable sets.
Distinct points have distinct coordinates; their lifts have coordinate spacing at least $X^{-2}$. A width-$w_j$ interval therefore contains at most $1+w_jX^2$ lifted points.
Takes the smaller of the coordinate-width bound and the perimeter-sensitive Fourier bound.

The identity $N_X=\sum_{c\le X}\varphi(c)$ and $\varphi(c)\le c$ give $N_X\le X^2$ for $X\ge1$. This elementary upper bound is used in the small-perimeter examples and repeated in the lower distance estimate.
A segment starting at $(1/X,1/X)$ captures both one point and a number proportional to $pX^2$; division by $N_X$ gives the two terms in the lower bound. Integer parts handle real heights.
A path crossing the topological boundary bounds the symmetric difference by $B|h|_2^{\alpha}$; the translation lemma and smooth brackets then give shell norms uniformly in alpha.
Uses the explicit geometric-series constants for exponents in compact positive ranges, and treats $\beta=1/3-\alpha/2$ directly through zero with a logarithmic cutoff factor.
Combines the pointwise discrepancy reduction, boundary-based bracket norms, arithmetic shell estimate and uniform dyadic sums before optimizing delta.
Separates a strip near the unit-square boundary from interior discs to obtain $b_{\pi\Omega}(s)\le(8+4\gamma)s$ at small s, and an admissible global constant $B=8(1+\gamma)$ for alpha one.
The construction arcs give a covering by $O((\ell/s)^d)$ discs of radius $O(s)$, yielding boundary-tube order at most $s^{2-d}$; the source's dimension d also obstructs a linear tube bound.
Definition of well-shaped sets
Koch construction and Minkowski dimension

Bracket the convex indicator pointwise, use the nonnegative coefficients $|a_X(k)|^2$ in the difference identity, sum the squared shell estimates, and take $\delta=(8X)^{-1}$ to obtain the convex clause of Theorem 1.5.

Direct integration gives the nonzero coefficient of an arc indicator as an endpoint exponential difference divided by $2\pi i m$. Its modulus is bounded by the smaller of the arc length and $(\pi|m|)^{-1}$; the zero coefficient is the length.

Use products of arc brackets and dyadic blocks in each frequency separately. Proposition 2.3 and the resulting one-variable sums, with $\delta=(16X^2)^{-1}$, give the area-dependent rectangle clause of Theorem 1.5.
The exact relation $\nu_X=(1-N_X^{-1})\nu_X^*+N_X^{-1}\delta_0$ implies that the two probability measures differ on any measurable set by at most $N_X^{-1}\ll X^{-2}$.

Handle sets below the one-point threshold by the exact identity. Otherwise split at frequency $T=X^2/P$, use the convex Fourier tail above $T$, and pair the pointwise coefficient bound with the squared shell estimate below $T$.
Apply the established convex variance estimate with area $\pi r^2$ and perimeter $2\pi r$; discs of radius at most $1/4$ fit in a translated unit square.

Use the one-point identity for a side below $X^{-2}$. Otherwise factor the squared indicator coefficients, sum separate frequency blocks against Proposition 2.3, and split the one-variable sums at the reciprocal side lengths.

For $X>9$, the rectangle $[2X^{-1/2},3X^{-1/2}]\times[\tfrac15X^{-1/2},\tfrac14X^{-1/2}]$ has area $1/(20X)$ and contains no modular-inverse point. The proof separates points with $ab=1$ from those with $ab=1+jc$, $j\ge1$.

An empty disc forces normalized-count deviation $\pi r^2$. Chebyshev's inequality and the disc variance therefore bound the measure of $\{d_X>r\}$ by $\ll_\varepsilon X^\varepsilon(X^{-2}r^{-2}+X^{-5/3}r^{-2/3})$ for $0<r\le1/4$.
For any fixed $0<\kappa\le1/4$ and sufficiently large $X$, Corollary 1.3 ensures that every disc of radius $X^{-1/2+\kappa}$ contains a point. Hence $d_X(u)<X^{-1/2+\kappa}$ for every center.

Use the layer-cake formula, the trivial tail bound below $X^{-1}$, the variance tail up to $X^{-1/2+\kappa}$, and the vanishing tail beyond it. The integral of $r^{s-3}$ produces the three cases $s<2$, $s=2$, and $s>2$.

A union of $N_X$ discs covering at most half the torus gives a lower bound $\gg_sX^{-s}$. The middle quarter of the explicit empty rectangle has measure $\asymp X^{-1}$ and distance $\gg X^{-1/2}$ from the point set, giving $\gg_sX^{-1-s/2}$.
BRS Section 1.2 supplies the credited empty-box construction and the contextual discussion of smoothing the modulus cutoff.
